source_title: The front page of the Internet and 3 misconceptions about India - The Times of India
source_excerpt: This week, the World Bank released its latest Poverty and Equity Brief on India. Its headline finding is remarkable: India lifted about 50 crore people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023. Extreme poverty fell from 27.1 per cent to 2.6 per cent. The Bank called it one of the fastest poverty declines anywhere in the world.You would think a number like that would settle the argument over whether India's growth story is real. It will not. I spend a good part of my time on Reddit, which calls itself the front page of the internet, arguing about exactly this question. Reddit is anonymous, so nobody cares who you are and a comment rises or sinks on its merits alone. That makes it the most candid window I know into how people actually think, and a place Indian commentators, fixated on X, have largely ignored.What Reddit has taught me is that the case against India's growth story rests on three beliefs, and they arrive in a predictable sequence. When one is disproved, the argument simply retreats to the next.Misconception one: India is not really growingThe conversation usually starts here. The GDP numbers are fudged, the argument goes, and real growth is far lower, perhaps close to zero.This debate has largely been settled. India introduced a new GDP series in February 2026, moving the base year from 2011-12 to 2022-23. This October, Krishna Srinivasan, Director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, said the updated methodology fully matches the advice of the IMF's own statistics department and is consistent with good practice. A handful of commentators with books to sell still insist growth is a statistical illusion, but most people have learned to tune them out.The headline number also does not stand alone. Vehicle sales, electricity demand, GST collections, digital payment volumes and air passenger traffic all point the same way. These are recorded by crores of independent transactions every day and are very hard to fake.Misconception two: The gap between rich and poor is wideningHaving conceded growth, the argument shifts. Fine, the economy is growing, but the gains are going to the top.The same World Bank brief answers this. India's Gini index fell from 28.8 in 2011 to 23.0 in 2023. India is one of the rare countries that has grown rapidly while also reducing inequality.Present this number and the goalposts move. That is only consumption inequality, comes the reply, what about income? Show income, and the demand becomes wealth.But consumption is the standard measure of inequality in developing economies, not a convenient choice. Income is extraordinarily difficult to measure where most work is informal. Ask someone on the street what they earn and you are unlikely to get an accurate answer. You can, however, reliably record whether a household bought a two wheeler, a television or a refrigerator.The World Bank does caution that consumption surveys tend to understate spending by the very rich. That is fair. But what matters for a country of 140 crore people is what happens to the great mass of them, not how many cars India's billionaires buy. The fact that crores of families have bought their first two wheeler matters far more to India than the garages of a few billionaires.Misconception three: Everyone is getting poorerThis is the final retreat, and a remarkable one. First the claim was that nobody was getting richer. Then it was that the rich were pulling away. Now, with both disproved, the argument turns the first on its head: inequality is falling because the rich and the middle class are sliding down to meet the poor.This is where the World Bank's new numbers matter most. About 50 crore people do not climb out of poverty in an economy where everyone is getting poorer. The Bank attributes the decline mainly to strong consumption growth, rising employment, particularly among women, and expanded social transfers. That describes people moving up, not a society sinking together.Look at what India's poorest households now own. According to data compiled by the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister, in 2011-12 only about 6 per cent of the poorest 40 per cent of rural households owned a motorcycle or a car. By 2023-24, 47 per cent did. In cities, the share rose from 20 to 60 per cent. Fridge ownership among the rural poor went from 3 per cent to 23 per cent, and mobile phones are now near universal. That is the opposite of a society sliding down to meet the poor. The 50 crore people leaving poverty are joining the middle class from below.Clear the ground firstNone of this should be controversial, yet a large and articulate section of people believe the opposite of all three: that Indians are not getting richer, that the gap between rich and poor is widening, and that everyone is getting poorer. They are living in a different India from the one the data describes.For economists, intellectuals and commentators, dismantling these three beliefs is the first job, because a positive story about India bounces off a reader who carries them. A democracy cannot be strong unless its citizens are willing to accept facts as they are, regardless of who gets the credit for them, and regardless of whether someone we dislike had a hand in them. Reddit is very good at showing you what people believe. It cannot make them look further. The front page of the internet can only invite you to open the book. It is your responsibility to read through it and imbibe the lessons. The World Bank has just added a new chapter, and it is worth reading.(Anuj Gupta is Managing Director, India, at BowerGroupAsia.)Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.
